name: Alfred the Great
summary: King of the West Saxons who resisted the Viking Great Heathen Army, secured the Danelaw frontier and promoted learning and law. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Edward the Elder
summary: Son of Alfred who conquered much of the southern Danelaw and extended West Saxon overlordship over Mercia. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: AElfweard of Wessex
summary: Son of Edward the Elder who may have reigned in Wessex for a few weeks in 924; his kingship is disputed. Dates are received from chronicle tradition.

name: AEthelstan
summary: First king to rule all England, victor at Brunanburh in 937 and a major legislator. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Edmund I
summary: Half-brother of AEthelstan who recovered the Five Boroughs from Norse rule; murdered at Pucklechurch. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Eadred
summary: King who finally ended the Norse kingdom of York with the death of Eric Bloodaxe in 954. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Eadwig
summary: Teenage king whose reign saw conflict with Dunstan and the loss of Mercia and Northumbria to his brother Edgar. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Edgar the Peaceful
summary: King associated with the Benedictine reform, monetary reform and a famous imperial coronation at Bath in 973. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Edward the Martyr
summary: Young king murdered at Corfe in 978 and swiftly venerated as a saint. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: AEthelred the Unready
summary: Long reign dominated by renewed Viking invasions, Danegeld payments and the St Brice's Day massacre; driven out by Sweyn Forkbeard in 1013. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Sweyn Forkbeard
summary: Danish king who conquered England in 1013 and reigned for a few weeks before dying at Gainsborough. Dates are received from chronicle tradition.

name: AEthelred the Unready (restored)
summary: Second reign of AEthelred after Sweyn's death, ending with his own death in London amid Cnut's invasion. Regnal dates are those received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later chronicles and may be uncertain by a year or more.

name: Edmund Ironside
summary: Warrior son of AEthelred who fought Cnut to a partition of England at Olney and died months later. Dates are received from chronicle tradition.

name: Cnut the Great
summary: Danish conqueror who ruled England, Denmark and Norway as a North Sea empire and governed England through native institutions. Dates are received from chronicle tradition.

name: Harold Harefoot
summary: Son of Cnut who ruled England, first as regent then as king, against the claims of his half-brother Harthacnut. Dates received from chronicles.

name: Harthacnut
summary: Son of Cnut and Emma who united the English and Danish crowns briefly and died suddenly at Lambeth. Dates received from chronicles.

name: Edward the Confessor
summary: Restored king of the house of Wessex, builder of Westminster Abbey, whose childless death triggered the succession crisis of 1066. Dates received from chronicles.

name: Harold Godwinson
summary: Last crowned Anglo-Saxon king of England; won at Stamford Bridge and was killed at Hastings on 14 October 1066.

name: Edgar the AEtheling
summary: Last male of the house of Wessex, proclaimed king in London after Hastings but never crowned; submitted to William at Berkhamsted.

name: William I the Conqueror
summary: Duke of Normandy who conquered England in 1066, imposed Norman lordship, built castles and commissioned Domesday Book.

name: William II Rufus
summary: Second Norman king, quarrelsome with the Church and killed by an arrow in the New Forest.

name: Henry I
summary: Youngest son of the Conqueror who took England and Normandy, issued the Charter of Liberties and left a disputed succession after his son's death.

name: Stephen
summary: Nephew of Henry I whose contested accession produced the civil war known as the Anarchy; agreed to be succeeded by Henry of Anjou.

name: Empress Matilda
summary: Daughter of Henry I who controlled England briefly in 1141 as Lady of the English but was never crowned queen.

name: Henry II
summary: First Plantagenet king, ruler of a vast Angevin domain, reformer of English common law and antagonist of Thomas Becket.

name: Richard I the Lionheart
summary: Crusader king who spent almost his entire reign abroad on the Third Crusade and in continental war, dying at Chalus.

name: John
summary: Lost Normandy to Philip II, quarrelled with the papacy and was forced to seal Magna Carta in 1215.

name: Henry III
summary: Boy king whose long reign saw baronial reform, the Provisions of Oxford, the Second Barons' War and the rebuilding of Westminster Abbey.

name: Edward I
summary: Conqueror of Wales, campaigner in Scotland and summoner of the Model Parliament of 1295.

name: Edward II
summary: Defeated at Bannockburn and dominated by favourites; deposed in 1327 and died at Berkeley Castle.

name: Edward III
summary: Claimed the French throne and opened the Hundred Years War, won Crecy and Poitiers, and ruled through the Black Death.

name: Richard II
summary: Faced the Peasants' Revolt as a boy and later ruled autocratically; deposed by Henry Bolingbroke in 1399.

name: Henry IV
summary: First Lancastrian king, who usurped Richard II and spent his reign suppressing rebellion including Glyndwr's rising and the Percys.

name: Henry V
summary: Victor of Agincourt in 1415 whose Treaty of Troyes made him heir to France; died of dysentery in 1422.

name: Henry VI
summary: Inherited England and the French claim as an infant; his incapacity and factionalism led to the loss of France and the Wars of the Roses.

name: Edward IV (first reign)
summary: Yorkist king who seized the throne after Towton and was driven out in 1470 by Warwick and the Lancastrians.

name: Henry VI (restoration)
summary: Brief Lancastrian restoration engineered by the Earl of Warwick, ending with Barnet, Tewkesbury and Henry's death in the Tower.

name: Edward IV (second reign)
summary: Restored Yorkist rule, stabilised royal finances and reigned in comparative peace until his sudden death in 1483.

name: Edward V
summary: Boy king deposed after eleven weeks by his uncle Richard of Gloucester; one of the Princes in the Tower, never crowned.

name: Richard III
summary: Last Yorkist and last Plantagenet king, killed at Bosworth in 1485; his remains were found in Leicester in 2012.

name: Henry VII
summary: First Tudor king, who won at Bosworth, married Elizabeth of York and restored royal finances and authority.

name: Henry VIII
summary: Broke with Rome to become Supreme Head of the Church of England, dissolved the monasteries and married six times.

name: Edward VI
summary: Boy king under Somerset and Northumberland whose reign pushed England towards full Protestantism and the Books of Common Prayer.

name: Lady Jane Grey
summary: Proclaimed queen for nine to thirteen days in July 1553 under Northumberland's scheme; deposed by Mary I and later executed.

name: Mary I
summary: Restored Roman Catholicism, married Philip II of Spain and presided over the Marian persecutions.

name: Philip of Spain as King of England
summary: Jure uxoris king alongside Mary I under the terms of their marriage treaty; his title lapsed on her death.

name: Elizabeth I
summary: Last Tudor monarch, whose long reign saw the Elizabethan religious settlement, the defeat of the Spanish Armada and a literary golden age.

name: James I of England and VI of Scotland
summary: First Stuart king of England, uniting the English and Scottish crowns in his person and sponsoring the Authorised Version of the Bible.

name: Charles I
summary: Rule by personal prerogative and religious policy provoked the Civil Wars; tried and executed in Whitehall in January 1649.

name: Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector
summary: Head of state of the Protectorate over England, Scotland and Ireland after dissolving the Rump Parliament; refused the crown in 1657.

name: Richard Cromwell as Lord Protector
summary: Succeeded his father but lacked army support and resigned in May 1659, opening the way to the Restoration.

name: Charles II
summary: Restored Stuart king whose reign covered the Great Plague, the Fire of London, the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis.

name: James II of England and VII of Scotland
summary: Catholic king deposed by the Glorious Revolution after alienating the political nation; fled to France in December 1688.

name: William III
summary: Dutch stadtholder invited to rule jointly with Mary II; accepted the Bill of Rights and led the Grand Alliance against Louis XIV.

name: Mary II
summary: Joint sovereign with her husband William III after the Glorious Revolution; died of smallpox in 1694.

name: Anne, Queen of England, Scotland and Ireland
summary: Last Stuart monarch, who reigned over separate English and Scottish kingdoms until the Acts of Union created Great Britain in 1707.

name: Kenneth I MacAlpin
summary: Traditionally the first king of a united Picto-Gaelic kingdom of Alba, though the union was a longer process than the king-lists suggest. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Donald I
summary: Brother of Kenneth I, remembered for promulgating the 'laws of Aed' in Alba. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Constantine I
summary: King of Alba during heavy Viking pressure; killed fighting Norse raiders. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Aed
summary: Brief-reigning king of Alba, killed after about a year. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Giric
summary: King of Alba whose relationship to the Alpinid line is obscure; may have ruled jointly with Eochaid. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Eochaid
summary: Grandson of Kenneth I recorded as ruling Alba, perhaps jointly with Giric. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Donald II
summary: First king styled ri Alban, king of Alba, in the annals. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Constantine II
summary: Long-reigning king who fought AEthelstan and lost at Brunanburh, later retiring to St Andrews. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Malcolm I
summary: King of Alba who received Strathclyde or Cumbria from the English and raided Northumbria. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Indulf
summary: King of Alba during whose reign Edinburgh was said to have been taken from the Northumbrians. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Dub
summary: King of Alba killed in the dynastic feuding between the rival Alpinid branches. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Cuilen
summary: King of Alba killed by the men of Strathclyde. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Kenneth II
summary: King of Alba who raided Northumbria and was killed in a dynastic conspiracy. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Amlaib
summary: Brother of Cuilen recorded as briefly ruling Alba in opposition to Kenneth II. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Constantine III
summary: Short-reigning king of Alba killed in the continuing dynastic feud. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Kenneth III
summary: King of Alba killed at Monzievaird by his successor Malcolm II. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Malcolm II
summary: King who won at Carham in 1018, securing Lothian, and extended Scottish authority southwards. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Duncan I
summary: Grandson of Malcolm II whose failed campaigns ended with his killing by Macbeth. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Macbeth
summary: King of Alba for seventeen years, remembered as a capable ruler who went on pilgrimage to Rome; killed at Lumphanan. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Lulach
summary: Stepson of Macbeth, briefly king and killed in 1058. Dates are those received from later Scottish chronicle and king-list tradition and are not securely attested.

name: Malcolm III Canmore
summary: King who killed Macbeth's heir, married the Saxon princess Margaret and raided England repeatedly until his death at Alnwick.

name: Donald III Bane
summary: Brother of Malcolm III who twice seized the throne in reaction against Anglo-Norman influence; deposed and blinded.

name: Duncan II
summary: Son of Malcolm III installed with English help and killed within months.

name: Edgar
summary: Son of Malcolm III and Margaret, who ruled peacefully under English patronage.

name: Alexander I
summary: King who ruled southern Scotland while his brother David held the south-west; patron of the reformed Church.

name: David I
summary: Reforming king who introduced feudal tenure, burghs, sheriffs and a silver coinage, and invaded England during the Anarchy.

name: Malcolm IV
summary: Boy king known as the Maiden who ceded the northern English counties to Henry II.

name: William I the Lion
summary: Long-reigning king captured at Alnwick in 1174, whose Treaty of Falaise made Scotland briefly a fief of England.

name: Alexander II
summary: Settled the border by the Treaty of York in 1237 and extended royal power into the west.

name: Alexander III
summary: Won the Hebrides by the Treaty of Perth in 1266; his death without an heir precipitated the succession crisis.

name: Margaret, Maid of Norway
summary: Infant granddaughter of Alexander III recognised as heir; her death at sea in 1290 opened the Great Cause.

name: John Balliol
summary: Chosen king by Edward I's arbitration in the Great Cause and deposed after refusing English demands.

name: Robert I the Bruce
summary: Won Scottish independence at Bannockburn in 1314 and secured recognition by the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton.

name: David II
summary: Son of Bruce whose reign included defeat and long captivity in England after Neville's Cross.

name: Edward Balliol
summary: English-backed claimant crowned in 1332 who held parts of Scotland intermittently before abandoning his claim.

name: Robert II
summary: First Stewart king, nephew of David II, whose reign saw renewed border war with England.

name: Robert III
summary: Physically infirm king whose government was largely run by his brother the Duke of Albany.

name: James I of Scotland
summary: Held prisoner in England until 1424, then ruled forcefully at home; assassinated at Perth in 1437.

name: James II of Scotland
summary: Broke the power of the Black Douglases and was killed by an exploding cannon at Roxburgh.

name: James III of Scotland
summary: Unpopular king who pursued peace with England and was killed at Sauchieburn.

name: James IV of Scotland
summary: Renaissance king who married Margaret Tudor and died with much of his nobility at Flodden.

name: James V of Scotland
summary: King who allied with France, taxed the Church heavily and died shortly after the defeat at Solway Moss.

name: Mary, Queen of Scots
summary: Queen from six days old, briefly Queen of France, forced to abdicate in 1567 and later executed in England.

name: James VI of Scotland
summary: King of Scots from infancy who inherited England in 1603 and thereafter ruled both kingdoms from London.

name: Charles I of Scotland
summary: King of Scots whose prayer book policy provoked the Covenanting revolt and the Bishops' Wars.

name: Charles II of Scotland
summary: Proclaimed King of Scots in 1649 and crowned at Scone in 1651, though exiled until the Restoration of 1660.

name: James VII of Scotland
summary: Scottish reign of James II of England, ended when the Convention of Estates declared the throne forfeited.

name: William II and Mary II of Scotland
summary: Joint Scottish monarchs after the Revolution settlement, which also re-established Presbyterian church government.

name: Anne, Queen of Scots
summary: Last monarch of an independent Kingdom of Scotland before the Union of 1707.

name: Anne, Queen of Great Britain
summary: First sovereign of the united Kingdom of Great Britain, whose reign saw the War of the Spanish Succession and Marlborough's victories.

name: George I
summary: Elector of Hanover who succeeded under the Act of Settlement; his reign saw the 1715 Jacobite rising and the South Sea Bubble.

name: George II
summary: Last British monarch to lead troops in battle, at Dettingen in 1743; his reign covered the 1745 rising and the Seven Years War's opening.

name: George III
summary: Reigned through the loss of the American colonies, the union with Ireland and the wars with France, and suffered recurrent mental illness.

name: George IV
summary: Regent from 1811 and then king, famous for extravagance, patronage of the arts and the failed attempt to divorce Queen Caroline.

name: William IV
summary: Sailor king whose short reign saw the Great Reform Act, the abolition of slavery in the colonies and the new Poor Law.

name: Victoria
summary: Longest-reigning monarch until Elizabeth II, Empress of India from 1876, presiding over industrial and imperial expansion.

name: Edward VII
summary: First Saxe-Coburg-Gotha monarch, whose reign saw the Entente Cordiale and the constitutional clash over the People's Budget.

name: George V
summary: Reigned through the First World War, renamed the dynasty Windsor in 1917 and oversaw Irish partition and the first Labour government.

name: Edward VIII
summary: Reigned for 326 days in 1936 before abdicating to marry Wallis Simpson; later Duke of Windsor.

name: George VI
summary: Unexpected king who became a symbol of resistance in the Second World War and saw Indian independence and the founding of the NHS.

name: Elizabeth II
summary: Longest-reigning British monarch, presiding over decolonisation, the creation of the Commonwealth as a free association and seven decades of change.

name: Charles III
summary: Acceded on the death of Elizabeth II in September 2022 and was crowned in May 2023; reigning monarch of the United Kingdom.

name: Roman Britain
summary: The Roman province of Britannia, from the Claudian invasion of AD 43 to the effective end of imperial administration around 410.

name: Division of Britannia into provinces
summary: Severus divided Britain into Britannia Superior and Inferior; Diocletian later subdivided it further into a diocese of four or five provinces.

name: Sub-Roman Britain
summary: The period between the end of Roman rule and the Augustinian mission, marked by British kingdoms, Saxon settlement and very thin sources. Dating is conventional rather than exact.

name: Anglo-Saxon England
summary: The era of Germanic-speaking kingdoms in lowland Britain, from the traditional adventus Saxonum to the Norman Conquest. The start date is received tradition, not a fixed event.

name: The Heptarchy
summary: Conventional label for the seven principal Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, Kent, East Anglia, Essex and Sussex. The scheme is a later historiographical construct.

name: Kingdom of Wessex
summary: Kingdom of the West Saxons, founded according to tradition by Cerdic and Cynric, which under Alfred and his heirs became the nucleus of England. Foundation date is received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Mercia
summary: Midland kingdom dominant in the eighth century under Aethelbald and Offa, absorbed into the English realm after 918. Foundation date is first-attestation rather than calendar.

name: Kingdom of Northumbria
summary: Northern kingdom formed by the union of Bernicia and Deira, a centre of Insular learning, later a Viking kingdom of York. Dates are received from chronicle tradition.

name: Kingdom of Bernicia
summary: Northern Anglian kingdom between the Tees and the Forth, later joined with Deira to form Northumbria. Dates are received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Deira
summary: Anglian kingdom in what became Yorkshire, absorbed into Northumbria in the seventh century. Dates are received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Kent
summary: Earliest recorded Anglo-Saxon kingdom, traditionally founded by Hengist, first to be converted by Augustine's mission in 597. Foundation date is received tradition.

name: Kingdom of East Anglia
summary: Kingdom of the North and South Folk, home of the Sutton Hoo burial and the Wuffing dynasty, later part of the Danelaw. Dates are first-attestation approximations.

name: Kingdom of Essex
summary: Kingdom of the East Saxons, including London for a time, absorbed by Wessex in 825. Dates are received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Sussex
summary: Kingdom of the South Saxons, traditionally founded by AElle, annexed by Wessex in the ninth century. Foundation date is received tradition.

name: The Danelaw
summary: The area of eastern and northern England under Danish law and settlement after the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum, gradually reconquered by the West Saxon kings.

name: Kingdom of York (Jorvik)
summary: Norse kingdom centred on York, ruled by Viking kings until Eric Bloodaxe's expulsion and death in 954. Dates are received from chronicles.

name: Kingdom of England
summary: The English kingdom from AEthelstan's unification of the Anglo-Saxon realms to its merger with Scotland in the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707.

name: Kingdom of Scotland
summary: The Scottish kingdom, from the traditional union of Picts and Gaels under Kenneth MacAlpin to the Union of 1707. The foundation date is received tradition.

name: Pictland
summary: The kingdoms of the Picts north of the Forth, absorbed into the Gaelic-speaking kingdom of Alba during the ninth century. Dates are approximate and received.

name: Dal Riata
summary: Gaelic kingdom of Argyll and northern Ireland whose dynasty gave rise to the kings of Alba. Dates are received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Strathclyde
summary: Brittonic kingdom centred on Dumbarton and later Govan, absorbed into Scotland in the eleventh century. Dates are received and approximate.

name: Principality of Wales
summary: The Welsh principality of Gwynedd's rulers recognised as Princes of Wales, conquered by Edward I in 1283 and annexed to England by the Laws in Wales Acts.

name: Kingdom of Gwynedd
summary: The dominant kingdom of north Wales, whose rulers claimed the principality of Wales until Edward I's conquest. Foundation date is received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Powys
summary: Kingdom of eastern mid-Wales, later divided into Powys Fadog and Powys Wenwynwyn. Dates are received tradition.

name: Kingdom of Deheubarth
summary: South-western Welsh kingdom formed from Seisyllwg and Dyfed, prominent under Hywel Dda and Rhys ap Gruffydd. Dates are received tradition.

name: Laws in Wales Acts
summary: Tudor statutes annexing Wales to the realm of England, creating Welsh counties and parliamentary representation and making English the language of the courts.

name: Lordship of Ireland
summary: The papal-sanctioned lordship held by the kings of England after the Angevin invasion, effective authority often confined to the Pale.

name: Kingdom of Ireland
summary: Created by the Crown of Ireland Act of 1542, a client kingdom under the English and then British crown until the Union of 1801.

name: Gaelic Ireland
summary: The network of Irish kingdoms and lordships under Gaelic law, ending with the Nine Years War and the Flight of the Earls. Dates are approximate and received.

name: Commonwealth of England
summary: The republic established after the execution of Charles I, governing England, and after conquest Scotland and Ireland, until the Restoration.
aliases: Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland

name: The Protectorate
summary: Constitutional regime under the Instrument of Government in which Oliver and then Richard Cromwell governed as Lord Protector.

name: Kingdom of Great Britain
summary: State created by the Acts of Union of 1707 uniting England and Scotland under one parliament at Westminster, until the union with Ireland in 1801.

name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
summary: State created by the Acts of Union of 1800 and lasting until the secession of the Irish Free State in 1922.
aliases: UK of Great Britain and Ireland

name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
summary: The present United Kingdom, comprising England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, dating in its current form from the Irish Free State's separation in 1922.

name: British Empire
summary: The worldwide network of English and then British colonies, dominions and dependencies, conventionally dated from Elizabethan claims to the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.

name: First British Empire
summary: The Atlantic-focused empire of American colonies, Caribbean sugar islands and the slave trade, ending with American independence.

name: Second British Empire
summary: The eastward-facing empire centred on India, Africa and the settler dominions, at its greatest extent after the First World War.

name: Northern Ireland
summary: Constituted in 1921 from six Ulster counties under the Government of Ireland Act, remaining part of the United Kingdom after partition.

name: Irish Free State
summary: Dominion established by the Anglo-Irish Treaty, covering twenty-six counties, replaced by the constitution of Ireland in 1937.

name: Republic of Ireland
summary: The sovereign Irish state under the 1937 constitution, formally declared a republic and outside the Commonwealth in 1949.

name: Lordship and Crown Dependency of the Isle of Man
summary: Norse-Gaelic kingdom ceded to Scotland in 1266, later an English lordship and today a Crown Dependency with its own ancient parliament.

name: Lordship of the Isles
summary: MacDonald lordship dominating the Hebrides and west coast, forfeited to James IV in 1493.

name: Channel Islands (Bailiwicks of Jersey and Guernsey)
summary: Remnants of the Duchy of Normandy that stayed loyal to the English crown in 1204 and remain self-governing Crown Dependencies.

name: House of Wessex
summary: The Cerdicing dynasty of West Saxon kings who became kings of the English, ending with Edward the Confessor and Edgar the AEtheling. Foundation date is received tradition.

name: House of Denmark (Knytlinga) in England
summary: The Danish kings Sweyn, Cnut, Harold Harefoot and Harthacnut who ruled England as part of a North Sea empire. Dates received from chronicles.

name: House of Normandy
summary: The Norman dynasty of William I, William II, Henry I and Stephen of Blois that transformed English land tenure, law and architecture.

name: House of Plantagenet
summary: The Angevin and Plantagenet kings from Henry II to Richard III, under whom Parliament, common law and the Hundred Years War took shape.

name: House of Lancaster
summary: The cadet Plantagenet line of Henry IV, Henry V and Henry VI, symbolised by the red rose.

name: House of York
summary: The rival Plantagenet line of Edward IV, Edward V and Richard III, symbolised by the white rose.

name: House of Tudor
summary: The Welsh-descended dynasty of Henry VII to Elizabeth I, spanning the English Reformation and the growth of the Tudor state.

name: House of Stuart
summary: Dynasty of Scottish kings from Robert II which acquired England in 1603 and ended with Queen Anne; interrupted by the Interregnum and the Revolution.

name: House of Hanover
summary: The German-descended dynasty of the four Georges, William IV and Victoria, under which cabinet government and the empire matured.

name: House of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha
summary: The dynastic name inherited from Prince Albert, borne by Edward VII and briefly George V until it was changed in 1917.

name: House of Windsor
summary: The reigning royal house, renamed from Saxe-Coburg-Gotha by George V in July 1917 amid wartime anti-German feeling.

name: House of Blois
summary: The single-reign dynasty of King Stephen, whose disputed rule produced the Anarchy.

name: House of Dunkeld
summary: The Scottish royal line descended from Malcolm III and Duncan I that presided over the feudalisation of Scotland.

name: House of Alpin
summary: The Alpinid kings of Alba descended from Kenneth MacAlpin, ruling by alternating succession between two branches. Dates received from king-lists.

name: House of Balliol
summary: The rival royal line of John and Edward Balliol, sustained by English support against the Bruces.

name: House of Bruce
summary: The dynasty of Robert I and David II which secured Scottish independence.

name: House of Orange-Nassau in Britain
summary: The reign of William III, the only Dutch monarch of the British kingdoms, ruling first jointly with Mary II.

name: Jacobite line of succession
summary: The exiled Stuart claimants James II, James Francis Edward, Charles Edward and Henry Benedict, whose cause ended with the cardinal duke's death.

name: Robert Walpole
summary: Regarded as the first prime minister, Whig dominator of politics for two decades who kept Britain out of war until Jenkins' Ear.

name: Spencer Compton, Earl of Wilmington
summary: Nominal head of the ministry that succeeded Walpole, with real power held by Carteret and the Pelhams.

name: Henry Pelham
summary: Whig premier who ended the War of the Austrian Succession, reduced the debt and presided over the Broad Bottom ministry.

name: Thomas Pelham-Holles, Duke of Newcastle (first ministry)
summary: Succeeded his brother Henry Pelham but proved unable to manage the opening disasters of the Seven Years War.

name: William Cavendish, Duke of Devonshire
summary: Caretaker premier of the Pitt-Devonshire ministry during the crisis after the loss of Minorca.

name: Duke of Newcastle (second ministry)
summary: Partnership with Pitt the Elder that produced the victories of the annus mirabilis of 1759.

name: John Stuart, Earl of Bute
summary: Favourite of George III who concluded the Peace of Paris and resigned amid intense unpopularity.

name: George Grenville
summary: Premier responsible for the Stamp Act and the prosecution of John Wilkes.

name: Charles Watson-Wentworth, Marquess of Rockingham (first ministry)
summary: Whig ministry that repealed the Stamp Act while passing the Declaratory Act.

name: William Pitt the Elder, Earl of Chatham
summary: Architect of victory in the Seven Years War who as premier was incapacitated by illness.

name: Augustus FitzRoy, Duke of Grafton
summary: Led a divided ministry through the Wilkes affair and rising American discontent.

name: Frederick North, Lord North
summary: Premier throughout the American War of Independence, resigning after Yorktown.

name: Marquess of Rockingham (second ministry)
summary: Short second ministry that opened peace negotiations with America and passed Irish legislative independence; ended with his death.

name: William Petty, Earl of Shelburne
summary: Concluded the Peace of Paris recognising American independence.

name: William Cavendish-Bentinck, Duke of Portland (first ministry)
summary: Figurehead of the Fox-North coalition, dismissed by George III over the India Bill.

name: William Pitt the Younger (first ministry)
summary: Youngest prime minister at 24, reformer of finance and administration who led Britain into the French revolutionary wars; resigned over Catholic emancipation.

name: Henry Addington
summary: Negotiated the Peace of Amiens and resumed war before making way for Pitt's return.

name: William Pitt the Younger (second ministry)
summary: Formed the Third Coalition against Napoleon and died in office weeks after Austerlitz.

name: William Grenville, Lord Grenville
summary: Head of the Ministry of All the Talents, which abolished the British slave trade in 1807.

name: Duke of Portland (second ministry)
summary: Presided over the Peninsular War's opening and the Walcheren fiasco before ill health forced resignation.

name: Spencer Perceval
summary: The only British prime minister to be assassinated, shot in the lobby of the House of Commons in May 1812.

name: Robert Jenkinson, Earl of Liverpool
summary: Long-serving Tory premier through the defeat of Napoleon, Peterloo, repressive legislation and later liberal reform.

name: George Canning
summary: Shortest-serving prime minister, dying after 119 days in office.

name: Frederick Robinson, Viscount Goderich
summary: Unable to hold his coalition together and resigned without facing Parliament.

name: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington (first ministry)
summary: Victor of Waterloo who as premier reluctantly carried Catholic emancipation and opposed parliamentary reform.

name: Charles Grey, Earl Grey
summary: Whig premier who carried the Great Reform Act of 1832 and the abolition of slavery in the empire.

name: William Lamb, Viscount Melbourne (first ministry)
summary: Brief first ministry dismissed by William IV, the last time a monarch removed a premier commanding Commons support.

name: Duke of Wellington (caretaker ministry)
summary: Held office for about three weeks in November and December 1834 while Peel returned from Italy.

name: Robert Peel (first ministry)
summary: Minority ministry that issued the Tamworth Manifesto and fell after the 1835 election.

name: Viscount Melbourne (second ministry)
summary: Mentor to the young Queen Victoria, presiding over Chartist agitation and the new Poor Law.

name: Robert Peel (second ministry)
summary: Reformed tariffs and income tax, founded the modern police tradition and split his party by repealing the Corn Laws.

name: Lord John Russell (first ministry)
summary: Whig premier during the Great Irish Famine and the Public Health Act.

name: Edward Smith-Stanley, Earl of Derby (first ministry)
summary: Minority Conservative ministry known as the Who? Who? ministry.

name: George Hamilton-Gordon, Earl of Aberdeen
summary: Peelite-Whig coalition premier who took Britain into the Crimean War and fell over its mismanagement.

name: Henry Temple, Viscount Palmerston (first ministry)
summary: Brought the Crimean War to a close and suppressed the Indian Rebellion, ending Company rule.

name: Earl of Derby (second ministry)
summary: Minority ministry that transferred Indian government to the Crown and admitted Jews to Parliament.

name: Viscount Palmerston (second ministry)
summary: Steered neutrality in the American Civil War and died in office aged 81.

name: Earl Russell (second ministry)
summary: Attempted a new reform bill and resigned when it was defeated.

name: Earl of Derby (third ministry)
summary: Ministry that passed the Second Reform Act of 1867 nearly doubling the electorate.

name: Benjamin Disraeli (first ministry)
summary: Succeeded Derby and lost the general election within months.

name: William Ewart Gladstone (first ministry)
summary: Great reforming Liberal ministry: Irish disestablishment, the Education Act, the secret ballot and army and civil service reform.

name: Benjamin Disraeli (second ministry)
summary: Imperialist and social-reform ministry that bought Suez Canal shares and made Victoria Empress of India.

name: William Gladstone (second ministry)
summary: Third Reform Act, Egyptian occupation and the death of Gordon at Khartoum.

name: Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, Marquess of Salisbury (first ministry)
summary: First of three Conservative ministries by the last premier to lead from the House of Lords.

name: William Gladstone (third ministry)
summary: Introduced the First Irish Home Rule Bill, splitting the Liberal Party.

name: Marquess of Salisbury (second ministry)
summary: Unionist government of free education, county councils and the scramble for Africa.

name: William Gladstone (fourth ministry)
summary: Aged premier whose Second Home Rule Bill passed the Commons but was rejected by the Lords.

name: Archibald Primrose, Earl of Rosebery
summary: Liberal premier who introduced death duties and was undermined by party divisions.

name: Marquess of Salisbury (third ministry)
summary: Ministry of the Diamond Jubilee, imperial expansion and the Second Boer War.

name: Arthur Balfour
summary: Nephew of Salisbury whose ministry passed the 1902 Education Act and split over tariff reform.

name: Henry Campbell-Bannerman
summary: Liberal landslide premier who granted self-government to the Transvaal and began welfare legislation.

name: H. H. Asquith
summary: Presided over the People's Budget, the Parliament Act, the constitutional crisis over Ireland and the first half of the Great War.

name: David Lloyd George
summary: Dynamic wartime premier and peacemaker at Versailles, whose coalition ended with the Irish Treaty and the Chanak crisis.

name: Andrew Bonar Law
summary: Canadian-born Conservative premier who resigned after seven months with terminal illness.

name: Stanley Baldwin (first ministry)
summary: Called a snap election on protection and lost his majority.

name: Ramsay MacDonald (first ministry)
summary: First Labour prime minister, heading a minority government for nine months.

name: Stanley Baldwin (second ministry)
summary: Ministry of the return to the gold standard, the General Strike of 1926 and the equal franchise of 1928.

name: Ramsay MacDonald (second and National ministries)
summary: Labour premier overwhelmed by the slump who formed a National Government in 1931 and was expelled from his party.

name: Stanley Baldwin (third ministry)
summary: Managed the abdication crisis and began rearmament while pursuing conciliation abroad.

name: Neville Chamberlain
summary: Architect of appeasement and the Munich Agreement who declared war in 1939 and fell after the Norway debate.

name: Winston Churchill (wartime ministry)
summary: Led the wartime coalition to victory over Nazi Germany, defining British resolve in 1940.

name: Clement Attlee
summary: Built the welfare state and the NHS, nationalised key industries and granted independence to India.

name: Winston Churchill (peacetime ministry)
summary: Returned to office aged 76, ending rationing and accepting most of the postwar settlement.

name: Anthony Eden
summary: Premiership destroyed by the Suez Crisis of 1956.

name: Harold Macmillan
summary: Presided over affluence and decolonisation's wind of change, resigning amid the Profumo affair.

name: Alec Douglas-Home
summary: Renounced his peerage to lead the Conservatives and narrowly lost the 1964 election.

name: Harold Wilson (first ministries)
summary: Labour premier of devaluation, comprehensive education, Open University and the permissive social reforms of the 1960s.

name: Edward Heath
summary: Took Britain into the European Communities in 1973 and fell during the miners' strike and three-day week.

name: Harold Wilson (second ministries)
summary: Returned in 1974, held the 1975 referendum confirming EC membership and resigned unexpectedly in 1976.

name: James Callaghan
summary: Faced the IMF crisis and the Winter of Discontent, losing a confidence vote in 1979.

name: Margaret Thatcher
summary: First woman prime minister, who privatised industries, curbed the unions, won the Falklands War and reshaped British political economy.

name: John Major
summary: Signed the Maastricht Treaty, endured Black Wednesday and began the Northern Ireland peace process.

name: Tony Blair
summary: New Labour premier of devolution, the Good Friday Agreement, public spending growth and the Iraq War.

name: Gordon Brown
summary: Former chancellor whose premiership was dominated by the global financial crisis.

name: David Cameron
summary: Led coalition and then Conservative governments of austerity, the Scottish referendum and the Brexit referendum, resigning after the Leave vote.

name: Theresa May
summary: Sought to deliver Brexit but could not pass her withdrawal agreement through Parliament.

name: Boris Johnson
summary: Won a large majority on getting Brexit done, led the Covid-19 response and resigned amid successive scandals.

name: Liz Truss
summary: Shortest-serving prime minister, resigning after 49 days following the market reaction to her mini-budget.

name: Rishi Sunak
summary: First British Asian prime minister, governing amid inflation and losing the 2024 general election.

name: Keir Starmer
summary: Labour leader who won a landslide in July 2024 and is the incumbent prime minister.

name: Roman conquest of Britain
summary: Campaigns from Aulus Plautius' landing in AD 43 to Agricola's victory at Mons Graupius, bringing most of Britain under Rome.

name: Boudican revolt
summary: Iceni rising led by Boudica that destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before defeat at Watling Street.

name: Viking invasions of Britain
summary: Two and a half centuries of Scandinavian raiding, settlement and conquest, from Lindisfarne to Stamford Bridge. Start date received from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

name: Norman Conquest
summary: William of Normandy's invasion, victory at Hastings and subsequent subjugation of England, including the Harrying of the North.

name: The Anarchy
summary: Civil war between Stephen and Empress Matilda over the succession to Henry I, ended by the Treaty of Wallingford.

name: First Barons' War
summary: Rebellion against King John after Magna Carta, involving a French invasion, ended by the reissue of the charter under Henry III.

name: Second Barons' War
summary: Rising led by Simon de Montfort against Henry III, producing the parliament of 1265 before defeat at Evesham.

name: Edwardian conquest of Wales
summary: Edward I's campaigns ending Welsh independence with the death of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and a great programme of castle building.

name: First War of Scottish Independence
summary: War from Edward I's invasion through Wallace, Bruce and Bannockburn to the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton.

name: Second War of Scottish Independence
summary: Renewed conflict over the Balliol claim, including Neville's Cross and the captivity of David II.

name: Hundred Years' War
summary: Dynastic struggle between England and France over the French crown and Gascony, including Crecy, Poitiers, Agincourt and eventual English expulsion.

name: Glyndwr Rising
summary: Owain Glyndwr's national revolt against English rule, briefly establishing a Welsh parliament at Machynlleth.

name: Wars of the Roses
summary: Dynastic wars between Lancaster and York from St Albans to Stoke Field, ending with Tudor rule.

name: Anglo-Spanish War
summary: Undeclared war with Philip II including the Armada of 1588 and Drake's raids, settled by the Treaty of London.

name: Nine Years' War in Ireland
summary: Rebellion of Hugh O'Neill against Tudor rule, ending at Kinsale and Mellifont and opening the way to the Ulster plantation.

name: Bishops' Wars
summary: Scottish Covenanter resistance to Charles I's prayer book, whose cost forced him to recall Parliament.

name: First English Civil War
summary: War between King and Parliament from Edgehill to Naseby and the surrender of Oxford.

name: Second English Civil War
summary: Royalist and Scottish risings crushed at Preston, leading directly to the king's trial.

name: Third English Civil War
summary: Campaigns in Ireland and Scotland ending with Cromwell's victory at Worcester and Charles II's flight.

name: Wars of the Three Kingdoms
summary: The interlocking conflicts in England, Scotland and Ireland including the Civil Wars, Covenanter risings and the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland.

name: Cromwellian conquest of Ireland
summary: Parliamentarian reconquest marked by the sieges of Drogheda and Wexford and massive land confiscation.

name: Williamite War in Ireland
summary: War between Jacobite and Williamite forces including the Siege of Derry, the Boyne and Aughrim, ending with the Treaty of Limerick.

name: War of the Spanish Succession
summary: European war in which Marlborough won Blenheim and Ramillies, ending with the Treaty of Utrecht and the acquisition of Gibraltar.

name: Jacobite rising of 1689
summary: Highland rising for James VII including the victory at Killiecrankie and the massacre of Glencoe in 1692.

name: Jacobite rising of 1715
summary: The Fifteen, led by the Earl of Mar for the Old Pretender, halted at Sheriffmuir and Preston.

name: Jacobite rising of 1719
summary: Spanish-backed attempt defeated at Glen Shiel.

name: Jacobite rising of 1745
summary: The Forty-Five, in which Charles Edward Stuart advanced to Derby before annihilation at Culloden.

name: War of the Austrian Succession
summary: British participation against France and Prussia, including George II's victory at Dettingen.

name: Seven Years' War
summary: Global war in which Britain took Canada, expelled France from India and emerged as the leading colonial power.

name: American War of Independence
summary: Loss of the thirteen American colonies after Saratoga and Yorktown, recognised at the Peace of Paris.

name: Irish Rebellion of 1798
summary: United Irishmen rising inspired by revolutionary France, suppressed with great bloodshed and leading to the Union of 1801.

name: French Revolutionary Wars
summary: British participation in the coalitions against revolutionary France, including naval victories at the Nile and Camperdown.

name: Napoleonic Wars
summary: British-led coalitions against Napoleon, including Trafalgar in 1805, the Peninsular War and final victory at Waterloo.

name: Peninsular War
summary: Wellington's Iberian campaigns alongside Spanish and Portuguese forces, draining French strength.

name: War of 1812
summary: Anglo-American war fought in Canada and at sea, including the burning of Washington, settled by the Treaty of Ghent.

name: Crimean War
summary: Anglo-French war with Russia over the Ottoman Empire, remembered for Balaclava, Inkerman, Sevastopol and Florence Nightingale.

name: Indian Rebellion of 1857
summary: Great uprising against East India Company rule that led to direct Crown government of India.

name: First Boer War
summary: Transvaal war of independence ending in British defeat at Majuba Hill.

name: Second Boer War
summary: Long South African war involving sieges, guerrilla resistance, farm burning and concentration camps, ending at Vereeniging.

name: First World War
summary: British and imperial participation from the invasion of Belgium to the Armistice, with some 900,000 British and imperial dead.

name: Easter Rising
summary: Republican insurrection in Dublin, suppressed within a week, whose executions transformed Irish public opinion.

name: Irish War of Independence
summary: Guerrilla war between the IRA and Crown forces including the Black and Tans, ended by truce and the Anglo-Irish Treaty.

name: Irish Civil War
summary: Conflict between pro- and anti-Treaty forces over the settlement with Britain, won by the Free State government.

name: Second World War
summary: British and Commonwealth war against Germany, Italy and Japan, from Poland's invasion to VJ Day.

name: Battle of Britain
summary: Air campaign in which RAF Fighter Command defeated the Luftwaffe's bid for air superiority over southern England.

name: Dunkirk evacuation
summary: Operation Dynamo lifted some 338,000 Allied troops from Dunkirk in late May and early June 1940.

name: British involvement in the Korean War
summary: Commonwealth Division fought under United Nations command, notably at the Imjin River.

name: Suez Crisis
summary: Anglo-French-Israeli operation against Nasser's Egypt, abandoned under American and international pressure, exposing Britain's diminished power.

name: Malayan Emergency
summary: Long counter-insurgency campaign against communist guerrillas in Malaya.

name: Mau Mau Uprising
summary: Kenyan rebellion against colonial land policy, suppressed with mass detention and violence.

name: The Troubles
summary: Three decades of conflict in Northern Ireland between republicans, loyalists and the British state, ending with the Good Friday Agreement.

name: Bloody Sunday
summary: Paratroopers shot dead thirteen civil rights marchers in Derry on 30 January 1972, with a fourteenth dying later.

name: Falklands War
summary: Ten-week war to recover the Falkland Islands after the Argentine invasion of April 1982.

name: Gulf War
summary: British participation in Operation Granby, the coalition campaign to expel Iraq from Kuwait.

name: Iraq War
summary: Controversial British participation in the invasion and occupation of Iraq, later examined by the Chilcot Inquiry.

name: British involvement in the War in Afghanistan
summary: Combat operations, chiefly in Helmand, from the invasion of 2001 to the end of the combat mission in 2014.

name: Building of Hadrian's Wall
summary: Frontier wall from Tyne to Solway begun under Hadrian, later Rome's northern boundary in Britain.

name: Building of the Antonine Wall
summary: Turf frontier across the Forth-Clyde isthmus, occupied for barely a generation.

name: End of Roman rule in Britain
summary: Withdrawal of the last field armies and the traditional Rescript of Honorius telling the cities to look to their own defence. Dating is received tradition.

name: Gregorian mission of Augustine
summary: Augustine's arrival in Kent began the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons and the founding of the see of Canterbury. Date received from Bede.

name: Synod of Whitby
summary: Northumbrian council that adopted Roman rather than Irish practice for Easter and the tonsure. Date received from Bede.

name: Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum
summary: Agreement partitioning England between English and Danish rule along the Watling Street line. Dating is uncertain and received.

name: Unification of England under AEthelstan
summary: AEthelstan's takeover of Northumbria created a single kingdom of the English. Date received from chronicle tradition.

name: Domesday Book
summary: William I's great survey of landholding and resources in England, the most detailed record of its kind in medieval Europe.

name: Magna Carta
summary: Charter sealed by King John at Runnymede limiting royal arbitrariness and guaranteeing due process; reissued and enshrined in later law.

name: Provisions of Oxford
summary: Baronial reform programme imposed on Henry III establishing a council of fifteen and regular parliaments.

name: Provisions of Westminster
summary: Further baronial reforms addressing local administration and legal grievances.

name: Simon de Montfort's Parliament
summary: First English parliament to include elected burgesses from the towns as well as knights of the shire.

name: Model Parliament
summary: Edward I's assembly of lords, clergy, knights and burgesses, later seen as the pattern for Parliament.

name: Declaration of Arbroath
summary: Letter of the Scottish barons to the pope asserting Scotland's independence and the community of the realm.

name: Statute of Labourers
summary: Post-plague attempt to cap wages and bind labourers, a grievance behind the Peasants' Revolt.

name: Peasants' Revolt
summary: Rising against the poll tax and serfdom led by Wat Tyler and John Ball, suppressed after the confrontation at Smithfield.

name: English Reformation
summary: Break with Rome under Henry VIII, doctrinal change under Edward VI, Marian reversal and the Elizabethan settlement.

name: Act of Supremacy
summary: Statute declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head on earth of the Church of England.

name: Dissolution of the Monasteries
summary: Suppression of religious houses and transfer of their vast wealth to the Crown and its supporters.

name: Pilgrimage of Grace
summary: Northern rising against religious change and Cromwell's government, the greatest Tudor rebellion.

name: First Book of Common Prayer
summary: Cranmer's English liturgy, introduced by the Act of Uniformity and provoking the Western Rising.

name: Elizabethan Religious Settlement
summary: Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity establishing a Protestant church with the monarch as Supreme Governor.

name: Scottish Reformation
summary: Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction and adopted a reformed confession, founding the Kirk under Knox's influence.

name: Plantation of Ulster
summary: Organised settlement of English and Scottish Protestants on confiscated Ulster land, with enduring consequences.

name: Union of the Crowns
summary: James VI of Scotland's accession to the English throne joined the two crowns in one person while the kingdoms stayed separate.

name: Gunpowder Plot
summary: Catholic conspiracy to blow up the Palace of Westminster, foiled on 5 November 1605.

name: Petition of Right
summary: Parliamentary statement against non-parliamentary taxation, arbitrary imprisonment and billeting.

name: Personal Rule of Charles I
summary: Eleven years of government without Parliament, financed by ship money and marked by Laudian church policy.

name: Long Parliament
summary: Parliament summoned in 1640 that abolished the prerogative courts, tried Strafford and led the war against the king.

name: Trial and execution of Charles I
summary: The king was tried by a High Court of Justice and beheaded outside the Banqueting House on 30 January 1649.

name: Navigation Acts
summary: Series of laws reserving colonial trade to English and British shipping, a pillar of mercantilism until repeal.

name: Restoration of the Monarchy
summary: Charles II returned under the Declaration of Breda, restoring monarchy, Lords and the Church of England.

name: Great Plague of London
summary: Last major English bubonic plague epidemic, killing perhaps a quarter of London's population.

name: Great Fire of London
summary: Fire that destroyed much of the medieval City, prompting rebuilding in brick and Wren's churches.

name: Habeas Corpus Act
summary: Statute strengthening the writ against unlawful detention, a landmark of personal liberty.

name: Exclusion Crisis
summary: Attempts to bar the Catholic James from the succession, giving rise to the Whig and Tory parties.

name: Glorious Revolution
summary: Deposition of James II and accession of William and Mary on parliamentary terms, establishing constitutional monarchy.

name: Bill of Rights
summary: Statute limiting royal power, requiring frequent parliaments and free elections and barring Catholics from the throne.

name: Claim of Right
summary: Scottish counterpart to the Bill of Rights, declaring the throne forfeited by James VII.

name: Founding of the Bank of England
summary: Chartered to fund the war with France, creating the basis of the national debt and modern public finance.

name: Act of Settlement
summary: Vested the succession in Sophia of Hanover and her Protestant heirs and secured judicial tenure.

name: Acts of Union 1707
summary: Parallel Acts of the English and Scottish parliaments creating one Kingdom of Great Britain with a single parliament.

name: Septennial Act
summary: Extended the maximum life of a parliament from three years to seven.

name: South Sea Bubble
summary: Speculative collapse in South Sea Company shares that discredited ministers and elevated Walpole.

name: Highland Clearances
summary: Displacement of Highland tenantry for sheep and sporting estates, driving mass emigration. Dating is conventional.

name: Somerset v Stewart
summary: Mansfield's judgment that slavery had no positive law in England, freeing James Somerset.

name: Gordon Riots
summary: Anti-Catholic riots that overwhelmed London for a week, the worst civil disorder of the century.

name: Acts of Union 1800
summary: Legislation merging the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom from 1 January 1801.

name: Abolition of the Slave Trade Act
summary: Outlawed British participation in the transatlantic slave trade after two decades of abolitionist campaigning.

name: Peterloo Massacre
summary: Cavalry charged a mass meeting for parliamentary reform at St Peter's Field, Manchester, killing at least eleven.

name: Catholic Emancipation
summary: Roman Catholic Relief Act admitting Catholics to Parliament and most offices, conceded after O'Connell's Clare election.

name: Great Reform Act
summary: Redistributed seats, abolished rotten boroughs and extended the franchise to much of the middle class.

name: Slavery Abolition Act
summary: Abolished slavery across most of the empire from 1834, with apprenticeship and compensation to slave owners.

name: Poor Law Amendment Act
summary: Created the union workhouse system on principles of deterrence and less eligibility.

name: Chartism
summary: Mass working-class movement for the six points of the People's Charter, including universal male suffrage.

name: Repeal of the Corn Laws
summary: Peel's abolition of agricultural protection, embracing free trade and splitting the Conservative Party.

name: Great Exhibition
summary: Crystal Palace showcase of industry and empire in Hyde Park, visited by six million people.

name: Second Reform Act
summary: Extended the vote to urban working-class male householders, roughly doubling the electorate.

name: Elementary Education Act
summary: Forster's Act creating school boards and the framework of state elementary education.

name: Ballot Act
summary: Introduced secret voting in parliamentary and local elections, curbing intimidation.

name: Third Reform Act
summary: Extended household franchise to the counties, enfranchising agricultural labourers and miners.

name: Irish Home Rule Bills
summary: Successive attempts to grant Ireland a devolved parliament, twice defeated and finally enacted but suspended in 1914.

name: People's Budget
summary: Lloyd George's redistributive budget, rejected by the Lords and triggering the constitutional crisis.

name: Parliament Act 1911
summary: Removed the Lords' veto over money bills and replaced it with a delaying power, asserting Commons supremacy.

name: Women's suffrage movement
summary: Campaign of suffragists and suffragettes that won votes for women over thirty in 1918 and equal franchise in 1928.

name: Representation of the People Act 1918
summary: Gave the vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 with property qualifications, tripling the electorate.

name: Equal Franchise Act
summary: Gave women the vote on the same terms as men, at twenty-one.

name: Government of Ireland Act 1920
summary: Partitioned Ireland by creating separate parliaments for Northern and Southern Ireland.

name: Anglo-Irish Treaty
summary: Treaty of December 1921 creating the Irish Free State as a dominion, with Northern Ireland opting out.

name: Statute of Westminster
summary: Recognised legislative independence for the dominions, converting empire into Commonwealth.

name: Abdication Crisis
summary: Constitutional crisis over Edward VIII's wish to marry Wallis Simpson, ending in his abdication in December 1936.

name: Beveridge Report
summary: Social Insurance and Allied Services, the blueprint for the postwar welfare state and its attack on the five giants.

name: Education Act 1944
summary: Butler Act creating free secondary education for all and the tripartite system.

name: Founding of the National Health Service
summary: Bevan's NHS opened on 5 July 1948, providing healthcare free at the point of use across Britain.

name: Postwar nationalisations
summary: Attlee government took coal, rail, road haulage, electricity, gas, steel and the Bank of England into public ownership.

name: Arrival of the Empire Windrush
summary: The Windrush brought Caribbean migrants to Tilbury, a symbolic beginning of large-scale postwar Commonwealth immigration.

name: Decolonisation of the British Empire
summary: Withdrawal from India in 1947 through African independence in the 1960s to the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.

name: Independence and partition of India
summary: British withdrawal created India and Pakistan, with mass displacement and communal violence.

name: Founding of the modern Commonwealth
summary: The London Declaration made the Commonwealth a free association of equal states with the King as its head.

name: Accession to the European Communities
summary: Britain joined the EEC on 1 January 1973 after two French vetoes, confirmed by referendum in 1975.

name: 1975 European Communities referendum
summary: First UK-wide referendum, in which two thirds voted to stay in the European Communities.

name: Winter of Discontent
summary: Wave of public sector strikes against pay restraint that destroyed the Callaghan government's authority.

name: Miners' Strike
summary: Year-long strike against pit closures, defeated by the Thatcher government and decisive for union power.

name: Privatisation programme
summary: Sale of state industries including BT, British Gas, water, electricity and rail, reshaping the British economy.

name: Poll tax and its riots
summary: The Community Charge provoked mass non-payment and rioting, contributing to Thatcher's fall and its abolition.

name: Black Wednesday
summary: Sterling was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism on 16 September 1992, wrecking Conservative economic credibility.

name: Good Friday Agreement
summary: Settlement establishing power-sharing devolution, cross-border bodies and consent for constitutional change.

name: Devolution to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
summary: Referendums of 1997 and the Acts of 1998 created the Scottish Parliament, Welsh Assembly and Northern Ireland Assembly.

name: House of Lords Act 1999
summary: Removed all but ninety-two hereditary peers from the House of Lords.

name: Human Rights Act 1998
summary: Incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law.

name: Scottish independence referendum
summary: Scotland voted 55 to 45 per cent against independence on a record turnout.

name: Brexit referendum
summary: The UK voted by 52 to 48 per cent to leave the European Union on 23 June 2016.

name: Withdrawal from the European Union
summary: The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and the transition period ended on 31 December 2020 under a trade agreement.

name: Covid-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom
summary: National lockdowns, furlough, mass vaccination and more than 200,000 deaths involving the virus.

name: High Medieval England
summary: Era of Norman and Angevin consolidation, castle and cathedral building, common law, and population and town growth.

name: Black Death in England
summary: Plague that killed perhaps a third to a half of the population, transforming labour, wages and land tenure.

name: Late Medieval England
summary: Period of famine, plague, French war, peasant revolt and dynastic conflict.

name: Tudor Period
summary: Era of Reformation, state building, inflation, enclosure and Elizabethan expansion overseas.

name: Elizabethan Era
summary: Golden age of English drama and seafaring under Elizabeth I, with Shakespeare, Marlowe, Drake and the Armada.

name: Jacobean Era
summary: Reign of James I, marked by the King James Bible, Jacobean drama and early colonisation of Virginia.

name: Caroline Era
summary: Reign of Charles I before the Civil War, with Laudian church reform and personal rule.

name: Interregnum
summary: The republican years between the execution of Charles I and the Restoration, under Commonwealth and Protectorate.

name: Restoration Era
summary: Period of restored monarchy, Restoration comedy, the Royal Society, plague and fire.

name: Augustan Age
summary: Literary and political era of Pope, Swift and Addison, and of Whig oligarchy under Walpole.

name: Georgian Era
summary: Age of the four Georges and William IV, spanning agricultural improvement, empire, industrialisation and classical architecture.

name: Scottish Enlightenment
summary: Flowering of philosophy, economics and science in Edinburgh and Glasgow, with Hume, Smith, Black and Hutton.

name: British Agricultural Revolution
summary: Enclosure, crop rotation, selective breeding and improved yields that fed a rapidly growing urban population.

name: Industrial Revolution
summary: Transformation of Britain by steam power, factory textiles, coal, iron, canals and railways, the first industrial society.

name: Regency Era
summary: Formal regency of the Prince of Wales during George III's incapacity, byword for elegance, dandyism and Austen's novels.

name: Victorian Era
summary: Long age of industrial power, imperial expansion, urbanisation, reform and evangelical earnestness under Victoria.

name: Early Victorian Period
summary: Years of Chartism, railway mania, the Hungry Forties and the repeal of the Corn Laws.

name: Mid-Victorian Boom
summary: Era of prosperity, free trade and the workshop of the world, opened by the Great Exhibition.

name: Late Victorian Period
summary: The Long Depression, new imperialism, mass literacy and the rise of organised labour.

name: Great Famine in Ireland
summary: Potato blight and government policy produced about a million deaths and a million emigrants, halving Ireland's population over decades.

name: Edwardian Era
summary: Confident, unequal decade of Edward VII, with Liberal welfare reform and mounting industrial and constitutional conflict.

name: Interwar Period
summary: Years of demobilisation, the General Strike, the Depression, mass unemployment and appeasement.

name: General Strike
summary: Nine-day national strike in support of the miners, called off by the TUC without concessions.

name: Great Depression in Britain
summary: Slump that brought heavy unemployment to the industrial north and Wales, the Jarrow March and the abandonment of the gold standard.

name: The Blitz
summary: German bombing of British cities from September 1940 to May 1941, killing over 40,000 civilians and devastating London, Coventry and others.

name: Postwar Austerity
summary: Years of rationing, dollar shortage, the 1947 fuel crisis and reconstruction under the Attlee and Churchill governments.

name: Postwar Consensus
summary: Broad agreement across parties on the welfare state, full employment, mixed economy and union consultation.

name: Swinging Sixties
summary: Decade of British pop culture, fashion, the Beatles, permissive legislation and social liberalisation centred on London.

name: Thatcherism
summary: Programme of monetarism, privatisation, union curbs, deregulation and popular capitalism associated with Margaret Thatcher.

name: New Labour Era
summary: Third Way project of Blair and Brown: constitutional reform, public investment, market-friendly economics and foreign intervention.

name: Austerity
summary: Deficit-reduction programme of spending cuts and welfare reform after the financial crisis, under coalition and Conservative governments.

name: Brexit Era
